question_en: A fund manager is preparing a presentation that shows the fund's number of stock holdings per country and also categorizes the stocks by market cap. Which of the following data visualization tools is most appropriate to reflect this data?
option_a: Tree-map
option_b: Histogram
option_c: Scatterplot matrix
explanation_en: Data visualization tools display the frequency of categorical (ie, qualitative) or numerical (ie, quantitative) data points. Tree-maps visualize the frequency of categorical variables by using nested rectangles and can show joint frequencies across different levels of a hierarchy. In this scenario, the fund manager wants to simultaneously show the total number of stock holdings per country and the stock classifications by market cap. The frequency of each outcome of the first-level categorical variable (eg, country) is visualized using differently colored rectangles, with each rectangle's size proportional to the number of observations. Those rectangles are further divided into smaller rectangles, which group observations based on a second categorical variable and show the frequency of variable outcomes (eg, different market caps). In this way, tree- maps can display joint frequencies (eg, frequency by country and market cap) and accommodate as many levels of categorical data as needed. (Choice B) Histograms are used to display the frequency of numerical variables. They cannot be used with categorical variables. (Choice C) A scatterplot matrix is a collection of scatterplots in which each graph is used to examine the relationship between a different combination of two numerical variables. It cannot be used for categorical variables.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: Natural language processing is most appropriate for use when:
option_a: analysis is needed for large amounts of sensor-based data.
option_b: a company globally monitors employee emails for compliance.
option_c: the algorithm must generate predictions that are highly accurate.
explanation_en: Text analytics is a fintech application that analyzes text- and voice-based data. Natural language processing (NLP) is a category of text analytics that focuses mainly on developing algorithms and applications to interpret human language. NLP can enhance a company's compliance processes by automatically monitoring employee emails for word patterns that may flag compliance issues or even fraud. One limitation to NLP is that human language is imprecise; an algorithm may not be able to interpret idioms or distinguish true intent from sarcasm. NLP used to analyze emails does not necessarily conclude that fraud or noncompliance occurred. Instead, it allows humans to investigate further based on the initial algorithmic analysis. NLP may not be suitable for analysis that needs to convey very precise outputs or predictions (Choice C). (Choice A) Sensor-based data consists of items such as satellite imagery, climate and security updates for "smart" buildings, and smartphone images. This type of data typically does not involve human language, so NLP would not be useful.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: Machine learning may be most appropriate for data analysis if:
option_a: training data are applied to targeted outputs.
option_b: the input data have not been filtered to eliminate bias.
option_c: patterns from raw data inputs were obtained through supervised learning.
explanation_en: Types of machine learning (ML) Model specifies inputs and outputs ("labeled data") to train algorithm Supervised Algorithm predicts outcomes from new data sources Model does not specify outputs and uses unlabeled input data Unsupervised Algorithm attempts to find patterns or characteristics from raw data Can incorporate supervised or unsupervised ML Deep learning Uses multi-stage nonlinear data processing Machine learning (ML) is a subcategory of artificial intelligence in which computer programs "learn" to predict outcomes from inputs known as training data. "Fintech" is the term used to describe the integration of technology with financial services. It incorporates ML to analyze information from very large datasets, which the programs then use to predict outcomes. One type of ML model is created through supervised learning. Supervised learning refers to algorithms that map input data to specified outputs (ie, targeted outputs). Both the data and the targeted output are provided to the algorithm, which "learns" from subsequent input data. One example is using historical information correlated to stock prices to identify variables that predict price changes. The algorithm then uses changes in those variables to predict future stock prices (ie, targeted outputs). (Choice B) ML requires large amounts of data to be effective. The data must be as free as possible from bias (eg, sample bias, where the sample is not representative of the environment in which the algorithm will be running). In addition, it must not contain spurious data (eg, data that appear to be related but are not causally connected). (Choice C) Supervised learning specifies inputs and outputs that an algorithm uses to find patterns in new raw data sources. Unsupervised learning refers to ML models that determine patterns or characteristics from large amounts of raw input data without specified inputs or outputs. An unsupervised learning algorithm may be able to discern patterns from data that would not be obvious to humans.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: Use of fintech most appropriately enhances a company's risk analysis capabilities when:
option_a: machine learning analyzes input data for errors.
option_b: the data to be analyzed excludes quantitative data.
option_c: the risk analysis focuses mainly on market and trading risk rather than operational risk.
explanation_en: Fintech refers to technological innovation in designing and delivering financial information and products. One practical application of fintech concerns how investment companies can utilize machine learning to analyze and manage risk. Machine learning is the creation of algorithms that analyze enormous amounts of qualitative and quantitative input data to predict future outcomes or to identify patterns that would not otherwise be obvious. Risk analysis uses data from multiple sources, many of which are classified as alternative sources (eg, photographs, text messages). Machine learning is easily adapted to determine whether this data contains errors, bias, or outliers that would distort the predictive ability of a risk model that will use the data. In other words, if the data contains errors that were missed during human quality control processes, machine learning can help validate the data before it is used by the algorithm that manages risk. (Choice B) Risk management uses both quantitative and qualitative data. (Choice C) Operational risk is the risk of loss caused by failed systems or processes within the firm. Fintech can use algorithms that analyze a variety of input data to predict events that result in losses from operational risk.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: A corporate banking analyst is evaluating the concentration risk of a bank's lending portfolio jointly across countries and sectors. The analyst calculates the relative value of the loans (by country and sector) in proportion to the portfolio's value. Which of the following data visualization tools is most appropriate to reflect this data?
option_a: Heat map
option_b: Line chart
option_c: Scatterplot
explanation_en: The frequency of categorical (qualitative) or numerical (quantitative) data points can be summarized using data visualization tools. The joint frequencies of two categorical variables can be depicted using a heat map. Heat maps visualize relative magnitude using a color spectrum. One end of the color spectrum represents high-frequency data points; the opposite end represents low-frequency data points. Each cell is colored differently according to the corresponding frequency. Heat maps can also be used to visualize the correlation between two categorical variables. In this scenario, each loan is assessed for two categorical variables: the sector invested in and the country invested in. An analyst calculates the relative frequency for each possible combination of the two variables, represented by each loan's percentage of the total portfolio (based on the loan's nominal value) and allocated jointly to each sector and country. Data points on the color spectrum's high end are associated with a higher concentration risk in the corresponding markets. (Choice B) Line charts, such as frequency polygons, display the frequency of one variable only and therefore cannot show joint frequencies. In other applications, more than one variable can be accommodated by plotting multiple data sets separately in the same chart for comparison. (Choice C) A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables represented on the x-axis and the y-axis (eg, technology sector returns versus Dow Jones Industrial Average returns). However, the two axes form a numerical scale for data points, so the scatterplot cannot be used to present categorical variables.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: Big Data most likely:
option_a: excludes data generated from traditional sources.
option_b: excludes unstructured data and includes only structured data.
option_c: is typically composed of data sets generated at high velocities.
explanation_en: Overview of Big Data Traditional: includes financial reports, census reports Data sources Alternative: includes social media, sensor networks Volume: large number of data points Data set characteristics Velocity: high speed of data collection Variety: many different formats and sources Structured: tabular data with distinct fields (eg, address database) Data structure Unstructured: unorganized data not in tabular format (eg, audios) Semistructured: mixture of structured and unstructured formats Big Data is a term referring to enormous amounts of data generated by businesses, governments, and individuals that can be captured through sources that are either traditional (eg, census reports) or alternative (eg, social media posts) (Choice A). These data sets are typically characterized by high volume (data points), velocity (speed), and variety (formats). The data can be structured, unstructured, or semistructured (Choice B). Structured data is stored in a tabular format where a unique record is stored in each row and various fields are stored in each column. Unstructured data such as data from an audio file is not stored in a tabular form. Semistructured data is a combination of the two.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: When considering different sources of Big Data, structured data most likely includes:
option_a: computer spreadsheets of historic company information.
option_b: postings by users of consumer products on social media.
option_c: point-of-sale information transmitted by cash registers in stores.
explanation_en: Classifications of big data Traditional Prices of stock trades Company reports Sources Alternative Social media Satellite images Structured: Tabular depiction (eg, spreadsheets) Data types Unstructured: Requires additional applications such as image recognition software and use data Fintech refers to technological innovation in designing and delivering financial information and products. One area of fintech concerns ways to efficiently use data generated by businesses, governments, and individuals. This data can arise from both traditional and alternative information sources; collectively, this data is commonly referred to as Big Data. Big Data can be categorized as structured or unstructured. Structured data refers to data that can be easily stored in a database. Historical stock prices, company earnings. and economic statistics are examples of structured data. Unstructured data largely encompasses alternative data sources such as social media postings and transaction information from point-of-sale registers in retail stores (Choices B and C). Unstructured data requires special applications to process the information before investment professionals can use it.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: With respect to machine learning, a model is most likely underfitted when:
option_a: the underlying data set is too small to analyze.
option_b: the model treats true parameters as if they were noise (ie, insignificant datapoints).
option_c: the model treats noise (ie, insignificant datapoints) as if they were true parameters.
explanation_en: Potential errors in the machine learning process Treats insignificant parameters as significant parameters Overfit Results from overly precise analysis Treats significant parameters as insignificant parameters Underfit Results from overly simplistic analysis Machine learning (ML) uses algorithms to identify patterns and relationships from training data (ie, input data) to predict outcomes for other data sets. According to CFA Institute curriculum, "ML algorithms aim to 'find the pattern, apply the pattern.'" Analysts should be aware of errors that arise from overfitting or underfitting training data during the training process. Overfitting refers to putting undue weight on insignificant datapoints (ie, noise) and treating them as if they were significant (Choice C). It results from overly precise data analysis. False relationships or unsubstantiated patterns are drawn from the training data and may lead to prediction errors in the future. Underfitting refers to putting too little weight on true (ie, significant) parameters and treating them as if they were noise. It results from overly simplistic data analysis. Important relationships or patterns may be left undiscovered in the training data, which may lead to prediction errors in the future. (Choice A) Underfit does not refer to the size of the training data. It refers to how well the data is specified.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best describes fintech within the investment management industry? Fintech is:
option_a: the financial analysis of technology stocks.
option_b: a form of technical analysis used to determine the price of an asset.
option_c: the convergence of finance and technology that provides easier access to investment
explanation_en: The convergence of finance and technology is commonly known as fintech. Creators and users of fintech changed the investment management industry. For example, firms now use robo-advisers, which are automated client account management programs using preset algorithms. Investors using robo-advisers receive a portfolio that matches their objectives (ie, return) and constraints (ie, risks) with little human interaction. With more automation than traditional investing, fintech enables investors to have easier access to investment management. (Choices A and B) Fintech is the innovation in finance using advancements in technology. It is neither a financial analysis of technology stocks nor a form of technical analysis.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: With respect to Big Data, data related to the Internet of Things (IOT) is most likely generated through:
option_a: sensors.
option_b: individuals.
option_c: business processes.
explanation_en: Sources of alternative data Individuals Text messages, videos, photos, audio files Business processes Customer transactions, bank records, supply chain data Sensors Smartphones, satellites, Internet of Things (IOT) Big Data refers to the vast amount of data generated by businesses, governments, and individuals. This data can be captured from traditional or alternative sources. Traditional data can be obtained from publications such as company financial reports or government census reports. In contrast, alternative data are usually less structured and come from sources such as social media posts, sensors, and credit card transactions. According to CFA Institute curriculum, alternative data can be broken down into three categories: data generated by individuals, business processes, and sensors. Data from individuals include unstructured data from text messages, videos, photos, and online audio files (Choice B). Data from business processes include credit card information, bank records, and supply chain information (Choice C). Data from sensors come from devices such as smartphones, cameras, and satellites that are connected through a wireless network. Data from sensors has vastly expanded over the years due to the ongoing development of microprocessors and networking technology. This growth has spawned the Internet of Things (IOT), an information ecosystem comprising networks of physical devices stored in offices, homes, and cars that enable data sharing over network connections.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding machine learning?
option_a: A model is underfitted when it treats noise data as true parameters.
option_b: Supervised learning involves using algorithms to learn unlabeled data.
option_c: Training data sets help identify historical relationships between variables.
explanation_en: Machine learning types and purposes Type Purpose Training Uncover relationships between inputs and outputs within historical data Validation Validate relationships and fine-tune predictive model Testing Test predictive accuracy A machine learning (ML) model uses an algorithm to uncover patterns and relationships from one data set to predict outcomes associated with other data sets. The machine learning process segments data into the three subsets shown above. The training data set is used for identifying historical relationships between inputs and outputs. Once the algorithm is "trained," it is validated and tested for accuracy with other data sets. After testing, the ML model is ready for use. (Choice A) Underfitting and overfitting errors can emerge from the ML process. A model is underfitted when it treats true parameters as noise data and is overfitted when it treats noise data as true parameters. (Choice B) Computers may employ a supervised or unsupervised approach to machine learning. Supervised learning models relationships based on labeled training data (ie, the inputs and outputs are clearly labeled). Unsupervised learning models relationships based on unlabeled data, so the algorithm attempts to "guess" the pairing of the inputs with the outputs.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\1. Quantitative Methods\1.11 Introduction to Big Data Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: A machine learning model treats noise in a training data set as valid parameters and subsequently fails when applied in reality. This outcome is most likely a result of:
option_a: overfitting.
option_b: using structured data.
option_c: using unstructured data.
explanation_en: Potential errors in the machine learning process Treats insignificant parameters as significant parameters Overfit Results from overly precise analysis Treats significant parameters as insignificant parameters Underfit Results from overly simplistic analysis Machine learning (ML) uses algorithms to identify patterns and relationships from training data (ie, input data) to predict outcomes for other data sets. Once a pattern is identified in the training data, it is then validated and tested before being applied to real data. Analysts should be aware of errors that arise from overfitting or underfitting training data during the learning process. Overfitting happens when the algorithm identifies spurious relationships or patterns (ie, noise) as significant, and results in identifying invalid relationships when applied outside the training data. Underfitting happens when the algorithm puts too little weight on valid parameters and treats them as if they were noise. This overly simplistic data analysis results in important relationships or patterns left undiscovered, leading to prediction errors in the future. (Choices B and C) Structured and unstructured data are classifications of big data, not ML model errors. Structured data refers to data that can be easily stored in a database, such as historical stock prices, company earnings, or economic statistics. Unstructured data largely encompasses alternative data sources such as social media postings and transaction information from point-of-sale registers in retail stores.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: When comparing ethical standards with legal standards, which of the following statements is most appropriate?
option_a: Behavior that complies with ethical standards may not always be legal.
option_b: A code of ethics provides specific rules that exceed legal requirements.
option_c: Regulations codify ethical standards, so a separate code of ethics is not needed.
explanation_en: CFA Institute's curriculum repeatedly emphasizes that legal standards alone are insufficient to shape appropriate behavior among investment professionals. The reasons why include the following: Laws are often too narrow to adequately prohibit all improper behavior. Laws that curb improper behavior are often enacted long after the behavior is first observed; therefore, significant harm caused by the behavior can occur in the interim. Ethics are created to govern moral conduct, which holds members and candidates to a higher standard than required by laws and regulations. The curriculum acknowledges that acting ethically may require members and candidates to perform illegal actions. For example, reporting dishonest conduct (ie, "whistleblowing") may be illegal, but it is ethically appropriate. (Choice B) A code of ethics serves as a general guide for appropriate conduct. Specific rules are established by a standard of conduct, and the standard often clarifies a code of ethics. (Choice C) Although laws may codify ethical standards, not all legal conduct is ethical. For example, it may be legal to use material nonpublic information as a basis for investing, but it is not ethical conduct.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: A framework for ethical decision-making will most likely be effective when:
option_a: external stakeholders are considered.
option_b: only verifiable information is included.
option_c: the framework steps are followed in order.
explanation_en: The ethical decision-making framework is designed to help identify important factors in the decision-making process. After identifying relevant information, the next step is to consider situational influences, additional guidance or advice, and alternative actions and consequences. After a decision is made and implemented, the decision-maker should assess the outcome. One relevant factor is to identity all stakeholders (both internal and external) involved and the responsibilities that may be owed to each. It is also important to identify all potentially relevant facts of the situation, whether verifiable or not (Choice B), and any conflicts of interest, existing or potential, that impact this decision. Finally, it is important to identify the ethical principles that bear on the decision. The framework is presented as a guide to a decision-making process, and while it is presented in a logical order (identify, consider, decide, assess), the steps may be applied in any order in practice (Choice C). Some steps may be repeated. For example, considering alternative actions may lead to identifying additional stakeholders or ethical principles.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: Which of the following is most likely an appropriate goal of using an ethical decision-making framework?
option_a: Allow for potential unintended consequences
option_b: Justify the decision to a broad range of stakeholders
option_c: Minimize the perspectives included in the decision-making process
explanation_en: A decision-making framework broadens the decision maker's approach by helping identify all relevant facts, stakeholders, possible conflicts of interest, duties owed, and ethical principles involved in a decision. Once stakeholders have been identified, the framework encourages a decision maker to consider and include the stakeholders' multiple perspectives and concerns. Since a range of stakeholder concerns is included in the decision-making process, the decision maker can better justify the decision to stakeholders. (Choice A) A decision maker should try to minimize the potential for unintended consequences in order to avoid the possibility that one decision, in turn, will create new problems. (Choice C) Including multiple perspectives in the framework helps the decision maker consider factors that might otherwise be overlooked.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: Which of the following clauses in a corporate bond indenture is most likely a type of negative pledge clause?
option_a: Incurrence test
option_b: Pari passu clause
option_c: Cross-default clause
explanation_en: Bond indentures are legal contracts that define the relationship between bondholders and issuers. Indentures specify the features of the bond (eg, coupon rate, maturity date) as well as investor and issuer rights and obligations. For example, issuers are obligated to pay, and investors have the right to receive, interest and principal. There may be contingency provisions that give the issuer the right to retire (ie, call) the bond before maturity or give investors the right to convert the bond into stock. Protective covenants are indenture provisions designed to protect the bondholders. These provisions are categorized as either: affirmative covenants, which require issuers to take specific actions that support the value of the bonds, or negative covenants, which prohibit issuers from taking actions that might adversely affect the value of the bonds. An incurrence test is a negative covenant that prohibits actions such as dividend payments, share repurchases, or debt issuance unless issuers satisfy specified financial tests (eg, debt-to-EBITDA < 5). (Choice B) A pari passu (ie, from a Latin phrase meaning "equal footing") clause is an affirmative covenant requiring an issuer to give a bonds' holders treatment equal to that given holders of similar seniority debt securities from the same issuer. (Choice C) A cross-default clause is an affirmative covenant requiring an issuer to declare a bond in default, even in the absence of a failure to pay, if the issuer defaults on any other debt obligation.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: A Charterholder who lives and works in a country that adheres to a "suitability standard" recommends an investment that meets a client's long-term financial objectives. If there was an equally suitable investment that paid the Charterholder a lower fee, the adviser's conduct can be best described as:
option_a: legal and ethical.
option_b: legal but unethical.
option_c: illegal and unethical.
explanation_en: Instruments for compliance with professional ethics Instrument Owner Describes Code of ethics Professional organization Shared principles Standards of conduct Professional organization Minimally acceptable behavior Laws and regulations Government Legal limits of behavior Legal standards alone are insufficient to shape appropriate behavior among investment professionals. Laws are often too narrow to adequately prohibit all improper behavior and are often enacted after injury or damage has been done. Ethics are created to govern moral conduct, which holds Members and Candidates to a higher standard than required by laws and regulations. Ethical behaviors are those actions that conform to society's expectations for honesty, transparency, and fairness. They balance each person's self-interest with an awareness of how a person's actions affect others. CFA Institute has adopted the Code and Standards as its statement of shared principles, on the belief that ethics for the global investment industry should be universal rather than based on local laws or customs. Global ethical standards are intended to create trust and integrity throughout the global financial system. In this instance, a suitability standard is a legal obligation that requires just a minimal level of investment appropriateness without consideration for other factors (eg, fees paid to the adviser). In contrast, a fiduciary obligation requires the adviser to adhere to a higher standard that involves always serving the client's best interest, such as minimizing fees, all else being equal. Therefore, the Charterholder's actions were legal but unethical (Choices A and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: Which of the following best describes an illegal but ethical activity?
option_a: Whistle-blowers alerting authorities of corporate corruption.
option_b: An analyst acting on a tip from a corporate insider in the United States.
option_c: Managers sharing the firm's complete fee structure with potential clients and the public.
explanation_en: Legal vs. ethical behavior Legal Illegal Ethical Adviser discloses fees to client Whistle-blower exposes corruption but violates disclosure laws Unethical Adviser is not fiduciary where not required by law Insider trading (US) Laws are not the ideal means to prevent unethical behavior since they are geographically inconsistent, slow to be enacted, and subject to compliance. Financial regulations and securities laws define illegal activities. However, abiding by laws may or may not indicate ethical behavior, which extends beyond laws and includes adhering to societal expectations of right and wrong. Thus, conduct can be legal but unethical. Conversely, conduct can be ethical but illegal. An example of this is an act of civil disobedience, which calls attention to an unethical law yet may violate local laws. Similarly, whistle-blowers who call attention to a company's illegal activity may be violating disclosure laws. Although alerting authorities to wrongdoing is ethically correct, it may also be illegal. (Choice B) Using inside information to profit is morally wrong since perpetrators benefit to the detriment of others. This is true even where it is legal. In the United States, using material nonpublic information is both illegal and unethical since it violates local laws. (Choice C) Managers publicly sharing fee information is legal and ethical. Firms have certain legal obligations regarding disclosures, including fees. It is also ethically correct to ensure that clients have enough information to make an informed decision.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the Code of Ethics for the global investment profession?
option_a: To build trust with all market participants
option_b: To set the basis for laws and regulations
option_c: To determine minimally acceptable behaviors
explanation_en: Instruments for compliance with professional ethics Instrument Owner Describes Code of ethics Professional organization Shared principles Standards of conduct Professional organization Minimally acceptable behavior Laws and regulations Government Legal limits of behavior A code of ethics is a professional organization's statement of shared principles. It provides the moral compass for collective behavior. Ethical behaviors are those actions that conform to society's expectations for honesty, transparency, and fairness, balancing each person's self-interest with an awareness of how his or her actions affect others. CFA Institute has adopted the stance that ethics for the global investment industry should be universal and not based on local laws or customs. This ubiquity creates trust and integrity in the whole global financial system. As stated in one of the principles in the CFA Institute Code of Ethics: "Members and Candidates must: Promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society." A profession's code of ethics may or may not be accompanied by standards of conduct, whereas standards of conduct exist only to enhance their associated code of ethics. CFA Institute has adopted both in its Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct (the Code and Standards). CFA charterholders and Candidates are expected to know and comply with both. (Choice B) It is a government's responsibility to establish legal limits of behavior through laws and regulations. The belief system used to create these policies in one country may differ from that of another country and from the shared ethical principles of a global organization. (Choice C) Standards of conduct clarify the minimally acceptable behaviors required to conform to a profession's code of ethics and provide a guide to practicing its principles.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession - Answers.pdf
subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: If a professional organization has standards of conduct in addition to its code of ethics, the purpose of the standards is most likely to describe:
option_a: shared principles.
option_b: laws and regulations.
option_c: acceptable behaviors.
explanation_en: Instruments for compliance with professional ethics Instrument Owner Describes Code of ethics Professional organization Shared principles Standards of conduct Professional organization Minimally acceptable behavior Laws and regulations Government Legal limits of behavior A code of ethics is a professional organization's statement of shared principles. Standards of conduct provide a guide to practicing the principles outlined in the code of ethics. Standards of conduct also clarify the minimally acceptable behaviors required to conform to the code of ethics. Although not addressed directly in standards of conduct, adherence to civil laws and regulations may be the minimally acceptable behavior in some cases. Standards of conduct may be principle-based or rule-based. Principle-based standards are universally applicable to members of the profession and are based on the principles outlined in the code of ethics. Rule-based standards, while also relating to the principles in the code of ethics, are usually more narrowly applicable and specific to certain members or scenarios that may arise. A code of ethics may or may not be accompanied by standards of conduct whereas standards of conduct exist only to enhance their associated code of ethics. CFA Institute has adopted both a code of ethics and standards of conduct (the "Code and Standards"); CFA charterholders and candidates are expected to know and comply with both. (Choice A) Standards of conduct are used to describe minimally acceptable behaviors or practices, given the shared principles of the code of ethics. The code of ethics describes the shared principles. (Choice B) Standards of conduct do not describe civil laws and regulations.
